title: Spike Lee the filmmaker, Spike Lee the professor

commenti.body: That's right. I see his movies and style as a very complex combination of storytelling and essays about race and power structures. His movies are more than "movies". They are critical devices, didactic artifacts, almost contemporary art pieces with a resemblance of Brecht' strategies. That's why I think he's one of the most important contemporary authors of USA. And that's why his filmography is, a lot of the times, misunderstood by the mainstream and classic film critics, when is not frontally rejected because of the power interests it defies.
Can’t wait for high and low!

I think you’re right on the money about Spike Lee as a filmmaker. I recently watched Summer of Sam and thought it was fantastic. When I looked up discussions of the movie afterwards, I was a bit disappointed, but maybe not shocked to see that there were many comments lamenting that the movie wasn’t more about the Son of Sam murders and seemingly missing the point of what the movie was about. To me it was pretty clearly a movie where Spike Lee was lecturing how white communities scapegoat and aim their anger when they can’t pin something on Black people or other racial minorities.

Thanks for your comment. I haven’t seen a lot of his movies, eapecislly those from the 90s / 2000s. Reading the description of the one you mentioned makes me want to move it up to the list.

I think Lee is often misunderstood by critics due to his films refusing to abide by genre norms. He makes movies in his style, which is utterly unique, and that often critiques the very industry it exists in

I’ve always seen his films as educational efforts using a narrative format. In many he’s not even subtle about it which works just fine for me. Which is why I was so disappointed with Da 5 Bloods. Started off promising as a chance to have a look at the black experience in Vietnam and afterwards with a half century’s distance. Yet quickly turns into Rambo. Complete with the kind hearted Vietnamese prostitute and the daughter who tells her till now absent dad that she loves him after spending less than two minutes with him. Missed opportunity

He's not necessarily always wrong but him being overty preachy with his messages sometimes is counterproductive to what film as an art form should be, which is provoking ambiguity the audience is almost unsure of the intent of until they view it through the lens of their own lives. He has a point of view and he doesn't care what some of the audience may think, and that gets in the way of him telling a story at times. In a bubble I actually think one of his better films is Oldboy because he isn't trying to say any message, just tell a story- there's absolutely zero fat on that film, it's like good filmmaking 101- but everyone hated it because they compared it to the superior original even though they were different interpretations, so what do I know.
